## Introduction & background

Interview questions often combine fundamental components in weird ways to test intuition. A high-gain comparator fed a sine wave acts as a zero-crossing detector, turning smooth AC into a square wave. An op-amp with capacitor feedback and resistor input is an integrator, turning a square wave into a triangle wave. Most interestingly, a capacitor rapidly toggled between two nodes with switches transfers discrete packets of charge $Q = C \Delta V$. At high frequencies, this rapid charge transfer looks exactly like a continuous current, allowing a switched capacitor to perfectly emulate a physical resistor. This is how high-precision filters and ADCs are built inside silicon ICs where large physical resistors are impossible to manufacture.

## Core equations

Switched-Capacitor Equivalent Resistance:
$$R_{eq} = \frac{1}{C f_s}$$

## Activity

Paper, committed answers, then verify. (1) Fronczak I: high-gain comparator, − input grounded, sinusoid into + — draw the output exactly. (2) Fronczak I: a capacitor alternately switched between Vin and Vout at frequency fs — show it acts as a resistor and derive Req = 1/(C·fs). (3) Op-amp with capacitor feedback and resistor input, square wave in — draw the output and name the circuit. (4) If you skipped it [Day 18](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-18.md): Fronczak II's mirror + op-amp Io problem.
**Then:** build or Falstad (2) and watch the "resistor" value change as you change fs.
